Mr. Speaker, as the federal member representing the riding of St. Catharines I am naturally interested in any kind of legislation that affects the wine industry in the Niagara region. I have had the opportunity of reading the submission by the Brewers Association to the House of Commons Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. Both the wine and the beer industries stand to suffer from the introduction of indexation, a new means of cost taxing related to the consumer price index.
I spent the past weekend in the city of St. Catharines attending the Folk Arts Festival and I took the opportunity, as I very often do, of showing guests around the community, pointing out the natural beauty of the area. I was far too often faced with the question, why are there so many acres of abandoned vineyards, non-productive acres lying in waste? I admit that some of this production has been lost as a result of the expansion of urban centres, including that of St. Catharines, but many acres have been lost to productivity because of this government's lack of concern for agriculture in the Niagara peninsula. Many of these vineyards have been abandoned because of the shortsighted economic policies of this government, of which the excise tax was an example in the first place. The indexing of that excise tax simply represents a further aggravation of a glaring and blatant lack of concern on the part of this government for the grape growers and the wine industry in our community. On the one hand the government claims it is concerned about the Canadianization of agricultural products and industry, but this is Canadianization that has taken the form of lip service only. The government discriminates against the wine industry by indexing its costs to the consumer price index.
For those of you who say this is not a precedent, let me expand on that further. Not only is it a precedent, it is discriminatory. The Finance Department claims this is based on the formula that applies to indexation of personal income taxes and is, therefore, presumably not discriminatory. In response I say to you, Mr. Speaker, what utter rubbish and
9956

nonsense. The Canadian people can thank a great Canadian and former leader of this party, the Hon. Robert Stanfield, for having instigated the indexation of personal income taxes. That particular indexing is based on real wage gains, not on cost of living increases given to help track inflation. Had it been based on cost of living increases, most Canadians would now be employees of the Liberal government.
The indexation proposed by Bill C-57 is not based on that formula. The tax on beer, wines and spirits, if indexed to the consumer price index, and as it applies to the alcoholic beverage subgroup, is a good example of this fact. Let me illustrate this point.
As the price of beer rises, whether by reason of increases in the cost of production, the cost of ingredients or the cost of packaging, this government automatically takes an additional share. This government takes its share of the inflationary expectations of the industry. This government has inflationary expectations and by this indexing lends a hand to that inflation. This government is feeding on inflation.
It has been stated that the basic reason for this indexing is to protect government revenues from erosion which has come about as a result of inflation. It has already been shown, only too often, that this government does not have the strength to fight inflation. Worse than that, this indexing form of taxation erodes the will and the desire of the government to even attempt to fight against this higher cost of living facing all of us. As I demonstrated a moment ago, the indexation of the tax on alcoholic beverages is not comparable to indexation of personal income taxes. That being the case, it is discriminatory-
We have something that is far worse. What we are really talking about is the establishment, as we have suggested often here today, of a precedent in the form of taxation. This is a precedent which can be used by the present or any future government to index any tax in relation to the consumer price index. The government will and has said that this is not something that will or can be called a precedent. Any intelligent, thinking person knows better than that. How can a precedent not be a precedent when it is a precedent? If that is a tongue twister, I would like you to try to untangle some of the circumlocutions in the answers and responses of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) when he tries to explain that this is not a precedent.
I cannot expect some people to follow that form of argument, nor can I object too strongly to this proposed new form of taxation. Canadians expect their government to be responsible, to manage the nation's business effectively and to be fiscally circumspect. Canadians do not expect their government to lie back and say, as it does in this instance with this indexation, that inflation is running out of control, that the government has no policies to combat inflation and that as a result it is taking an attitude of "I'm all right, Jack". That kind of approach looks after the government first and the Canadian consumer last.
Further, in recognizing the importance of fiscal responsibility, the Fathers of Confederation left with this House of Commons responsibility for fiscal matters. In Bill C-57 this government is saying that the Minister of Finance does not need to consult the House on future increases in taxation of alcoholic beverages because taxation will automatically increase. As long as the present government is in power, we do not have to concern ourselves with the possibility of a decrease because the consumer price index will continue to rise to record heights. What we have is underhanded taxation without representation. I am sure all members of this House will agree that automation in industry is one thing, but automation in the field of taxation is quite another.
We have been awaiting a new budget since the Minister of Finance introduced his ill-fated budget of October, 1980. As we all know, the measures introduced at that time have failed to have an impact on ever-rising interest rates and our out-ofhand inflation. As we know, the minister is reluctant to present a new budget because that would be a public admission that the government has been inept at dealing with the economic situation which exists in this country today.
If Bill C-57 passes with Ways and Means motion No. 22 included in it, that will be a further indication of two major points. The first is that the government truly has been bankrupt and is bankrupt in its economic policy. The second is that the government will continue to shift the burden of fiscal mismanagement on to those who can least afford to pay. I shudder when I see so much hardship being inflicted on those who can least afford to pay. The hardship is inflicted on hard-working, honest people.
I would like to return to an earlier comment about the growing number of vineyards in the Niagara region which are now going out of production. The people of St. Catharines take pride in the wines of that area. We were delighted to see so many Canadians not only trying Ontario wines but also preferring them and representing them as having an improved taste culture which competes with that of imported wines. As indicated in the brewers' submission, according to surveys there has been a 1.8 per cent decline in wine sales in the period between April, 1980, and January, 1981, compared with the same period just one year ago, and beer sales dropped 3.6 per cent in the same period compared with the previous year. This decline is related directly to the excise tax this government imposed on those two beverage sale markets. If that decline in beer and wine sales continues, then both those industries will have to face up to far more serious problems than they had a year ago.
Let us carry this one step further by projecting beer and wine prices if Bill C-57 is approved. According to the Brewers' Association, in ten years' time beer will cost $23.64 for 24 bottles, almost one dollar per bottle, an increase of 157 per cent. In the first instance, wines generally were subject to a percentage increase of 155 per cent. Now wines generally will be subject to a further increase of 125 per cent over the next ten years. This surely is not acceptable to this House. I ask the
May 26, 1981

government, and particularly the Minister of Finance or his assistant, the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres). Is it this government's intention to put brewers and wine makers out of business? Is it their intention to kill that goose which lays the golden eggs and which produces so much revenue dollars to the government today? If it is, I would appreciate knowing sooner rather than later because we could then inform local manpower offices to be prepared for such an event.
Does the Minister of State for Finance know that in Ontario alone the wineries and the grape growers employ over 18,000 persons? Is that not a segment of the community worth considering? In its brief to the standing committee, the Canadian Wine Institute hit the nail on the head when it stated that neither winemaking nor grape growing is a profitable business. For the information of members of this House let me say that in so far as wine production is concerned, the net return is less than 5 per cent of the capital cost investment. That is not a great venture from a profit-making point of view. There are already declining sales and, thanks to that earlier 155 per cent increase in the excise tax announced last April, this cannot fail to continue as the government loads quarterly increases onto the retail cost of wine. With this decline will come the collapse of the smaller wine industries-the cottage wine industries-which have improved the taste and quality of domestic wines. It will also lead to lay-offs in the larger wine industries.
I spoke earlier of the fuel which indexation will add to the inflationary situation. We are not speaking just of increased retail costs for agricultural or alcohol products. We shall have a larger administrative cost and an administrative burden which will add enormously to the cost of operations of, for example, the various provincial liquor control boards and, I might add, to the expansion of paper work which most of us see as an ever-increasing problem. Every three months, new price lists will have to be prepared, circulated, distributed and posted. As is the case with respect to weekly interest rate announcements, consumers will be able to bank on increases in the cost of their alcoholic beverages. This will come to be an accepted thing. We are building yet another bureaucratic nightmare.
I would like to conclude by reinterating the points I have attempted to make in this House this evening. First, the indexing of the tax on the alcoholic beverage subgroup of the consumer price index is a recognition on the part of this government that it has failed in its economic policies and that it has given up trying to fight inflation. That is a defeatist approach in every sense of the word.
Second, that indexation is in itself inflationary and will simply add to the inflationary spiral and the inflationary expectations of Canadians. Their own government expects increases in the consumer price index, and it intends to profit by them.
Third, the indexing sets a dangerous precedent which will, just as surely as I stand here this evening, be adopted by other governments, and it will be adopted by this government in relation to other products.
Excise Tax
Fourth, the indexation is discriminatory as it presently stands, and damaging to the wine and beer industry in particular. I repeat my earlier question: if the government is trying to put those industries out of business, then let it be honest and say so rather than going through the long drawn out and painful process of eliminating them.
Finally, I want to say that it is most distressing to me to answer questions in my home town community of St. Catharines when asked about those abandoned vineyards. The proposed indexing formed part of my response, and I hope that this House will have the wisdom to reject the government's irresponsibility in this respect so that I will not be faced at some future date with the question: did they not once grow grapes here? That is the future if this government continues in its approach to the agricultural industry in the Niagara peninsula.
The government has shown little interest in the Niagara fruitlands. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Ostiguy) may be an embarrassment to the minister but he is a millstone around the necks of the grape growers of Niagara. Let us eliminate now this built-in conflict of interest and get rid of the consumer price indexing of government revenue.

In this country, Mr. Speaker, only the strong are going to survive. That is an old saying. The Spartans had a way of testing their boy babies by exposing them to the elements for a period of time and if they survived, they brought them back, suckled them and made them soldiers. I want to say here that it is not enough to be strong to survive; they have to be strong and rich to survive. They have to be part of the elite of the economic feudalism which this government is creating because the small guy cannot survive. I commented last week in this House that a friend of mine is paying $7,200 on his mortgage and he will buy nothing else except food, clothing and fuel, and when he buys that fuel, he is going to pay the full scope of taxes and when he buys that clothing, if it happens to be a polyester fibre or a derivative of the hydrocarbon industry, he is going to pay the tax. If he ever has money enough to put a rug in that house, he is going to pay two taxes, the wellhead tax on the gas from which the material is derived and then, after the rug is made, he will have to pay tax on the tax on the cost of production of the rug, thereby paying twice.
This, Mr. Speaker, is the most iniquitous tax structure that I have ever seen imposed in this land, and at the same time these taxes are coming in to fatten the revenues of this government which it will spend at will to open new offices in Moncton, Fredericton and Saint John, to hire more and more people to manage more and more regulations and to bring in more and more new programs at a time when they claim they are going to save money.
This is a government of which Canadians certainly cannot be proud and which they must look at with regret. This is the first time that any government, except in wartime, has passed on the full burden of taxation to production. They have passed it on to the farmers, fishermen and lumbermen. At a time when you cannot afford to build a home and perhaps not even buy one already built, these taxes are coming in as an inflationary factor in the ever growing cost of that home. With regard to the farmer, I have heard the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) make excuses for the price of food. I thought they were not paying any attention. They do not pay any attention but something is bothering them. It must be their own negligence getting to their conscience, their abandonment of their principles, of responsibility for farmers, fishermen and consumers, all of whom are hurt, every last one of them.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we have reached the point in the trucking industry where you cannot make a long-term contract for trucking, but you can get a contract if you are prepared to accept the increment in rate which the industry may deem to be required as a result of additional taxation. And of course fuel is a part of it. That is a rather unstable situation for a producer of goods to have to live with. Having taxed the raw material to make the fibre for the rug and then the rug itself, you tax the transportation fuel which takes the rug to its destination. When this is coupled with the taxes imposed at the provincial level, I wonder what the first tax now amounts to. It probably approaches 20 per cent instead of the percentage you thought it was going to be when you read the bill and said "here is a tax on an article used for production". It is a pyramid of taxation and it is feeding inflation. It is feeding an inflation which is not entirely the same as historic periods of inflation have been. One thing which is lacking in this inflationary period is a lack of goods. There are goods all over the place; every shelf is full. Merchants are trying to reduce their inventories at a very serious sacrifice of profits because they cannot afford to pay the interest rates on them. As we tax here, we are ensuring that there will not be money to buy these goods. We are enhancing the demands of the people of the country who feed on inflation and require more to survive, as we tax and tax more. There are other ways to combat this.
The provinces set an example in earlier crises in home construction by removing the tax on building materials. It happened, for example in the province of New Brunswick. It began to appear that the province was losing revenue which it could ill afford to lose and that it was not necessarily accomplishing the purpose it hoped to accomplish because of the contradictory measures of the federal government. So, here we go again; we are again discouraging purchasing at a time when our shelves are full.
We require a full and complete fiscal monetary policy. There is only one portion of the objective a government must reach for which is being satisfied by this bill and this instrument of taxation across the board. If the government constrains itself to its present expenditure guidelines, I suppose it will reduce the deficit. This of course will reduce the demand on the money market, this of course will in fact have a favourable impact upon inflation, but this is the only aspect of
May 26, 1981

it which can in any way slow down or tone down the inflationary expectations of this land.
It does not make much difference what we look at. When we start taxing hydrocarbons at the wellhead, we are raising the cost of virtually everything in the country. We are raising the cost of transportation, agriculture, fishing, forestry and highway construction, because we are raising the cost of asphalt. We are raising the cost of everything virtually because of our maximum dependence upon the imported or local hydrocarbons as resources.
I would like to ask a question because I do not know the full answer. Perhaps the member of the government who is responsible for the bill will be able to give me the answer in due time. I would like to make a fairyland assumption, for the moment. Let me assume that there were absolutely no taxes on gas or oil as it arrives at our shores. I ask the minister what would be the cost of gasoline at the pump if we bought S32 per barrel oil from Saudi Arabia and the federal government did not tax a whit. What would be the price of gasoline in that event? It would be a little higher than it is today, unless there is a very serious error in my calculations.
We have brought on a lot of these taxes on the assumption that the equalization of the cost of petroleum products in this land can be accomplished by federal taxation on petroleum. If the federal government abandoned taxation on petroleum products and allowed Saudi Arabian oil to come into the eastern refineries of Canada which serve that part of Canada east of the Ottawa valley, as they have traditionally, how much additional oil would be necessary? If there were no federal tax of any kind, I think it would be rather interesting to see how little more would be necessary.
We are now paying for the cheapest barrel of oil we can get, approximately $1.55 to $1.56 per gallon. When we relate that to a 35-gallon barrel of oil, how much more would we actually need without a federal tax? I think it would be revealing. I think the people of this nation, the farmers in particular, would find that the tax on the fuel they use in their fields is really not so much for equalization as it is to feed the hunger of the spending machine of the Liberal government.
We have heard the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) indicate many times that they would try to serve the people of the country. 1 plead with them to get down to fiscal monetary responsibility which is such that we do not have to tax the living daylights out of the people of this land.
On the one hand we say to the provinces, as one example, that we will charge them more for RCMP services. Then the minister responsible for that service is quoted in The Globe and Mail last week as saying that the provincial ministers will not negotiate. As soon as I read that article, I telephoned the minister in New Brunswick responsible for that, and he said, "That is outrageous nonsense. Certainly we have tried to negotiate. We have tried to obtain a gradual change in the charges of the federal government for the RCMP". Also he said that he had asked as well the preceding minister, the hon.

member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. All-mand) to respond.
In the negotiations in 1975 or 1976, it was agreed that the cost would go up by one percentage point per year. It went from 44 per cent to 45 per cent of the cost to 50 per cent to 51 per cent of the cost from that period until now. Now in one fell swoop the federal government, in its urge to save money, will charge the provinces another $100 million.
Not only does this bill impose additional taxes on the consumers of Canada, it imposes them at a time when the government is imposing upon the provinces further reason for them to tax by withdrawing its support from the programs to which they have been accustomed ever since the RCMP has rendered municipal and provincial services in co-operation with the federal government. The only portion which is negotiable is: "We will provide the service if you will pay us what we want". This is what the federal minister said to the provincial ministers responsible for police services. Those ministers are prepared to negotiate and to escalate into a fair position of cost-sharing for the RCMP.
We should look at the contradiction. We tax more here and we pay less to the provinces. So the taxpayer will be hooked twice; once here and once when the bigger bill is issued to the provinces.
Let us look at the extremes and the desperation. This is where shame must enter into the hearts of some supporters of the government. We will tax hospitals, hospital equipment, research equipment and health centre equipment at a time when the provinces are pleading with the federal government not to cut those block grants which are going to them. The provinces, out of their money, will be required to equip the hospitals, the universities or the research centres with the help of taxpayer dollars. Again the health units, which are the responsibility of the provincial governments, will be paying more money. We are taxing more, spending more, opening offices, reducing our cost-sharing payments to the provinces and hitting the taxpayer coming and going, as we escalate taxes and increase prices and charges to the provincial governments. Why is this necessary?
Today the fishermen of this land are buying virtually all of their nets from Japan. With just a little care and caution in its price system, Mr. Speaker, do you realize that Japan can make those fishing nets cheaper than our fibre manufacturers can make them with the wellhead tax and the other taxes which have been applied to the hydrocarbons which are necessary to make those fibres? Japan imports all of its oil and gas. On top of that, we will be taxing these nets. By refusing to pass this tax on to the producers of goods and services in this country, we are denying them our own Canadian markets and leaving them vulnerable to countries which, with just a little price manipulation, can produce those fibres from hydrocarbons and their derivatives cheaper than we can produce them, though they import every single barrel of petroleum they need and every bubble of gas. This is what we are doing to our land. We

are not only taxing the consumer, we are taxing the producer. We are taxing the producer of goods in this country to the point where he may well be deprived of his own country's market. That is carrying it too far, Mr. Speaker. Yes, there is no question or doubt, only the strong can survive, if they are rich.
Before this bill goes further, and before some of those who are listening tonight give consideration to a favourable vote in support of this bill, I wish to remind this House once more that a combination of the inflationary structures in the agricultural community in which I live, plus the increments in interest which are being paid bankers, means that the cost of interest on the cost of processing potatoes has gone up tenfold, and it has risen fifteenfold on seed potatoes in a ten-year period. I am not one who gives a lot of statistics, but I promise members of this House that I can put those figures down in black and white for any individual who wishes to question my contention. There is not much difference between the costs incurred by the potato industry and those incurred by the fishermen. When will this government turn around and recognize that there are little guys buying homes and tractors, producing food, fishing for food, and that by helping them it can also help the consumer? The government might also make a contribution to reducing inflation if it would open fewer offices and allow more people to be employed in the private sector.

Mr. Speaker, I join in the debate this evening to side with my colleagues who have expressed concern about the provisions of Bill C-57. Some of our concerns have been expressed by and large in the amendments which have been placed on the Order Paper and which we are now debating. We hope that the government will give recognition to some of the arguments made by members on this side of the House. We feel that the amendments put forward are important and would serve the legislation and the country well.
Several of my colleagues have talked about the indexing provisions which have been introduced for the first time in regard to excise taxes at the federal level, the indexing of taxes on alcohol and tobacco. It is passing strange, if not alarming, to listen day after day to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) when he is questioned about interest rates and their high level. He is asked to take action to reduce these interest rates, and his answer to recommendations of members on this side is usually along the line, "Well, in an era of high inflation we have no choice. We have high inflation because of people's expectations. Because prices are going up, people expect high inflation, therefore they are borrowing money and, therefore, in order to limit the money supply, we must keep our interest rates high."
It is no wonder that people who have high expectations in terms of inflation expect it to continue when they see this government bringing in legislation which it says it must have in order to protect its revenues. In fact, that is inflationary. One day the Minister of Finance will criticize workers and unions who look for cost-of-living clauses in their contracts. He indicates that these kinds of provisions are inflationary, this
sort of indexing of salaries is inflationary. Yet, the next day he introduces legislation to index his own revenue sources. It is no wonder that any rational observer looking at the performance of this minister will conclude that there is no way the minister and the government will attack inflation. What they are attempting to do is to protect their revenues upon which the government operates, basically the same way as an individual or business operates to protect himself. This government is not acting on behalf of the nation as a trustee. It is operating as a corporate entity on its own in competition with the private sector. Just as the private sector moves to protect its welfare from inflation by raising prices, so does the government move to protect itself from inflation. The same is true for an individual who seeks to protect his salary from inflation.
The government is supposed to adopt the role of a trustee in terms of the rest of the population. It is not supposed to be competing with the private sector. It is not supposed to be designing systems to ensure that it can continue to extract funds from the private sector. It is supposed to be concerned about the whole country. But that is not the way this government behaves. Instead of acting responsibly by coming forward annually with a budget to raise or lower taxes according to need in an open and forthright manner, the government resorts to ploys such as the ones before us to index its revenue sources so that it will be protected. It does this to avoid the embarrassment and political cost of having to be open and honest about its revenue sources.
I would ask the government to re-examine its intent. I know that it has looked at the province of Quebec, the province of Ontario and others. The government says, "if the provinces are doing this, then why shouldn't we?" One good reason why the government should not is that it is supposed to be the national government, it is supposed to provide leadership. It cannot, on the one hand, demand more power from the provinces and on the other follow the bad examples set by those provinces which have resorted to indexation to protect their revenues.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 13, in Hansard, at page 9191, I asked the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) questions regarding the
May 26, 1981

auto parts manufacturers in Canada and the discussions the minister had with the U.S. government authorities when he visited Washington to pursue amendments to the auto pact. I asked as well if the minister had discussions with Japanese and European government trade officials regarding their automobile exports to Canada. We all realize the automobile industry and its component parts is having a difficult time. We all know as well that the solution is not an easy one.
All North American manufacturers of automobiles are coming out of a year of massive losses, coupled with the very high cost of tooling required to produce smaller fuel efficient cars. So one can see quite readily that a fast solution will not be found. Only time and a change in buyer preference will turn around this industry. Most manufacturers are producing their version of the world car. Industry spokesmen tell us that by the end of this decade there will be only five major automobile manufacturers left in the world. There may be a few smaller manufacturers producing for a local market; but the industry experts say there will be only five major manufacturers in 1990. I believe that is a valid analysis.
We hear every month about joint projects such as Volkswagen and Renault co-operating to design an automatic transmission that will be used by both manufacturers. We have also heard of Volvo and Renault developing a fuel efficient gasoline engine that will be used by both manufacturers. We see as well that Honda and British Leyland have an agreement to use Honda components with British Leyland sheet metal work and body, and so on.
We see these agreements and arrangements being made by various manufacturers because the cost for one of them to do it is tremendous, but two of them can share the cost and benefit from it. This is driving the industry together. The point of my question is, what is Canada doing to get some of the world car component parts business because the world car will be the volume car of the future? Can we get some of the component parts business? What can we get? In Burlington at the Oakville plant there is a very aggressive company called Tridon Limited. Tridon, after many years of research and development, is in the production of two very saleable items. One is a windshield wiper and the other is a flasher. It is selling that windshield wiper in 43 different countries in the world to original equipment manufacturers and to users as well.
The point is, what are the prospects for Canadian businessmen developing other products that could be used in world car production? This is the way we have to look. If we do not look at the world car market and try to get a piece of it, by the end of the decade our auto parts business will be simply non-existent.	.
A look at the auto parts industry in Canada will show that 70 per cent of the production facilities are subsidiaries of U.S. companies. Many of them have no sales force, and are really a manufacturing facility which builds on demand for the U.S. parent. I make no comment as to whether this is good or bad, only that it is hardly an atmosphere in which one could likely get component parts business for the world car market. We have had ample evidence from past history where development
Adjournment Debate
funds have been given to a company who has used those funds to develop a product, only to have the venture close down and production transferred to the foreign parent. I know we can all catalogue such cases.
I believe there is a place for Canadian components on the world car market. We have leverage because we have a good sized market of our own here. I believe we are the fifth or sixth largest user of Japanese automobiles. That is a sizeable market. We must not abandon this market or allow it to slip from our hands and go across the border in the reconstitution of the North American automobile industry.
We have heard very little, if anything, from the minister. He roars and he issues press releases which get headlines, but that is about all we see. All we have heard from the Washington talks is that the Americans feel it is not an opportune time to renegotiate the auto pact agreement. I believe that secretly industry, trade and commerce officials agree with that assessment. Fresh on the heels of press releases and headlines about a reduction in quotas of Japanese cars is a story that the Japanese will ask for a 5 to 8 per cent increase over last year. While the minister flops from one disaster to another, the opportunities of the world car slip from our hands forever. There is a market there. Tridon and others have proved it can be done.
I feel that this whole matter is lost in the depths of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and that we are only reacting to crises as they surface. The automobile industry contributes substantially to the economy of Canada.
I urge the minister to recognize the potential of the world car component parts business and to encourage and assist the automotive parts manufacturers to get a sizeable share for Canada.

One major effect of the auto pact has been the rationalization of the industry resulting in its transformation from a basic domestic supplier to a North American one for both original equipment and replacement markets. That was to the benefit of Canadian industry.
In relation to manufacturing, the automotive parts industry consists of four types of companies: divisions of U.S. auto manufacturers; foreign-owned multinational divisions; Canadi-

an-owned multinational companies; and wholly-owned Canadian companies.
In the first two groups, the disposition of funds rests largely in the U.S. to the extent that financial resources generated by U.S. branch plants cannot be regarded as always being available for use in Canada and in such activities as developing new markets, research and development, purchases of advanced equipment, or generally accommodating the Canadian operation to changing market conditions.
As the world car concept advances, rationalization on a world scale will affect various divisions of U.S. vehicle manufacturers. As an example, suspension components for the General Motors J-Car will be produced in only two GM plants in the world, one of which is located in Canada.

Indeed, some time early in the new year, additional funding was provided to this program, at least in my constituency.
The arguments I want to put before the minister tonight relate to how the program will be carried out this coming fall because there has been a wide variation in the amount of funding over the past three or four years. In the year 1980-81, under this program $376,373 was provided to the constituency
of Algoma. When the Conservatives were in power in 1980, no funding was provided under the Canada Works program. In the year 1978-79, my constituency received $1.5 million and in 1977-78, $1.8 million.
This program of employment during the winter months when there are high seasonal lay-offs is very important. It does not so much affect the communities in my constituency with a large industry such as a steel mill, a pulp and paper mill or a uranium mine, but it does affect the dozens of smaller villages, hamlets and rural townships throughout the vast area, some 400 miles in the Algoma-Manitoulin area.
Many of these communities have high seasonal lay-offs and the people are unable to find other work. Some must apply for unemployment insurance benefits or welfare. This is certainly true in the 12 Indian bands in the constituency.
My request to the minister tonight is that adequate funding be provided in the upcoming year for the community development program. Indeed, I hope there will be increased funding and that it will be targeted to the high unemployment areas of the country. Last year funding was provided right across the country, $100,000 to every constitutency whether it was needed or not. I feel that the program operated in 1978-79 which was targeted to the high unemployment areas was much more useful and beneficial.
It is important to note that over the past four or five years of this program the department has developed an excellent staff of young people who are dedicated, helpful and imaginative. They have developed a lot of expertise at operating direct employment programs. These people are available. There is a certain amount of additional overhead by having capable, competent staff like that, but it really pays off in value for the dollar spent. Often we are just displacing dollars that would be spent on welfare or unemployment insurance. People want to see value for the money spent for the work that is carried out.
I hope the minister will be successful when he puts this program before cabinet and that cabinet will hear these representations and will provide adequate funding for the community development program in the coming winter months. I hope the application forms will soon be made available in order that they can be processed over the summer months so that the projects can be approved, started on time and carried out during the winter months, providing much-needed employment in many of the slow growth areas of our country, at the same time carrying out very worth-while community projects, such as community halls, fire halls, and any number of other worth-while community projects carried out under this program over the last several years.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications; Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: EMPLOYMENT-INQUIRY RESPECTING INCREASE IN FUNDING OF COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that the hon. member in his question has acknowledged the extent of the response across the country to the Canada community development projects.
May 26, 1981

As the hon. member is aware, the government decided, immediately upon taking office, to initiate this direct job-creation program as a replacement for the Canada Works program which had been terminated by the previous government.
Through this program, $105.5 million was originally made available for the creation of jobs with a particular impact on the winter months of 1980-81. Early in this calendar year, an additional $4.5 million was made available to the program for the creation of additional employment opportunities. While these jobs were created across the country, they were concentrated in those areas and groups beset by high unemployment. As a result of this government's initiative, almost 20,000 people worked over the winter months who would otherwise have been unemployed. Some 60 per cent, or almost 12,000, of these persons are still working today.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: EXCISE TAX-APPLICATION TO LIQUOR SALES-PURPOSE OF INDEXATION
EXCISE TAX-APPLICATION TO LIQUOR SALES-PURPOSE OF INDEXATION
speechtext:
I rise in respect of a question I addressed to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) on May 15, and I submit the answer given was not only unsatisfactory but, perhaps, by a sin of omission was misleading to the House. I am in the hands of the Chair in that regard, but I suggest the minister misled the House in saying that the excise tax on alcoholic beverages to the alcoholic beverages subgroup, having regard to the consumer price index sale, was not discriminatory. Specifically the minister stated that a different tax system, an ad valorem tax system, applied to other commodities. This suggests that although we are talking about two different and separate tax systems, the end result is the same. That suggestion is unmitigated nonsense and I am surprised it should come from the Minister of Finance.
Perhaps it is best that I begin by trying to distinguish between these two systems and establish what we are talking about when we refer to an ad valorem tax and indexation. An ad valorem tax simply establishes the tax percentage rate applicable to a particular commodity. It is voted on in Parliament and the taxation rate does not change unless Parliament changes it, either by way of increasing or decreasing it. As the value of that particular commodity changes, the amount of tax may change but the applicable percentage rate does not.
Indexation on the other hand, as it applies in this case to the consumer price index, represents an entirely new trend in taxation policy. It sets a precedent which I find reprehensible. The percentage rate of taxation is pegged to the consumer price index, meaning that the government's percentage of taxation increases at a rate equal to the change or the increase in the consumer price index. What makes this so disturbing is that the change in percentage, unlike an ad valorem tax, is accomplished without parliamentary approval.
With the definition of these terms somewhat clarified, I should like to again refer to my question to the minister, pointing out that it was based on fact. The indexation of the excise tax on alcoholic beverages is discriminatory. No other
Adjournment Debate
tax is based on the consumer price index, and if the minister honestly believes that the effect of this taxation will be the same as an ad valorem tax, I invite him to make it an ad valorem tax so that the taxes all fall within the same system.
Of course the reason this was not made an ad valorem tax is that these are different tax systems, and the net return from indexation of the tax to the consumer price index will be far greater with the increase in consumer price index than it would have been on an ad valorem basis. It is the government's greed which has singled out these industries for this kind of tax. It is an established fact that beer and wine sales are down. My expectation in this regard is that this decline in sales will continue as long as this government continues to burden industries with higher retail costs as a result of a higher form of taxation.
The consumer, already in a financial squeeze, will simply cut back his or her purchases of alcoholic beverages. To an already closely run industry, a further drop in sales could only have a disastrous effect. If the government does not care about the wine or beer industries in particular, then let me add that the government is actively promoting inflation and inflationary expectations by the application of this indexing method.
Canadians expect interest rates to go up every week. This proposed indexation will give them a second expectation, and that is that every three months the cost of alcoholic beverages as a result of the indexed tax will increase as well.
I ask the parliamentary secretary, or whoever is speaking tonight on behalf of the Minister of Finance: does the minister propose to extend this precedent to other commodities, just as I indicated he might be able to do-and he can do-as he has in connection with the beverages we are talking about this evening? If he does not propose to add a form of indexing to other commodities, then how can he justify this continued discrimination against the wine, beer and spirit industries, particularly in view of the fact that they are now facing undue hardships?

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Stollery (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State and Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications; Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: EXCISE TAX-APPLICATION TO LIQUOR SALES-PURPOSE OF INDEXATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid) sought an explanation of the taxes on alcoholic beverages in his questions to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) on May 15, 1981.
The Excise Act and the Excise Tax Act impose commodity taxes on most goods imported into or manufactured in Canada. The great majority of these taxes are ad valorem levies; that is to say, they are expressed as a percentage on the sale price. The federal sales tax which is the main levy, is imposed at the rate of 9 per cent on most goods, except building materials, which are subject to a 5 per cent rate.
Since the federal sales tax is a percentage of the price, it automatically increases as prices increase. No special mechanism is required to achieve that relationship. Indeed, the system has functioned in that manner for more than 75 years.

May 26, 1981
Adjournment Debate
However, in the case of alcoholic beverages and tobacco products the commodity tax levies are structured somewhat differently. The bulk of the taxes on these goods are not expressed as a percentage of the price. Rather, they are expressed as an amount per unit of product. To illustrate, the levy on spirits was $16.25 per proof gallon of alcohol, and the levy on beer was 42 cents per gallon. These specific levies were increased in April, 1980 to $17.15 per gallon for spirits and to 54 cents per gallon for beer.
In the absence of discreet changes in such specific levies on alcoholic beverages, their real value falls as prices rise. Even with the increase in April, 1980, the real value of taxes on these goods is less than it was in the late 1960s.
Federal revenues should keep up with the growth in prices of products, as do those provincial mark-ups which are expressed
in percentage terms, and as does the general sales tax which is imposed on most goods as a percentage of value.
For these reasons, the government introduced a measure to adjust automatically the levies on alcoholic beverages in line with changes in prices. While this change does increase federal taxes on these products, it does not discriminate against beer, wines and spirits. Rather, it places the commodity tax levies on those goods on approximately the same basis as the commodity tax levies on all other goods.
